newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish unemployment seen falling before EU entry.
newsitem.headline: Polish unemployment seen falling before EU entry.

text.p: Poland's economic growth and foreign investment should bring its unemployment rate well within present European Union levels by 2002, when the country hopes to join the EU, economists said on Monday.

Janusz Witkowski, deputy-head of the Central Statistical Office (GUS), said that if Poland continued to grow at annual rates of five to six percent until EU entry, the number of jobless would shrink by a third from two million at the end of 1996.

"Poland's unemployment rate can be cut to some 8.0 to 8.5 percent, using international labour criteria, by the time the country enters the EU...which could realistically happen around 2002," Witkowski said in an interview.
This would place Poland in the middle of the current 15 EU member states, some of which have failed to stem growing jobless numbers.
According to Labour Force Survey (LFS) data, Poland's unemployment rate fell to 11.6 percent last November, from 13.1 percent a year earlier and a high of 14.9 percent in 1993.

Official figures from the labour ministry, whose jobless criteria have changed several times making it difficult to judge longer-term trends, showed 2.3 million people, or 13.6 percent of the workforce, unemployed at the end of 1996.

"If growth trends continue, Poland's unemployment rate could fall by as much as one percent per year ahead of EU entry...to around eight or nine percent," said Bohdan Wyznikiewicz, deputy president of the independent Institute for Market Economy Research (IBnGR).
Poland's unemployment surged after the fall of communism about eight years ago as overstaffed state firms laid off workers or went bankrupt when they lost government subsidies.
Analysts said economic growth and foreign direct investment would create new jobs, while training and extended schooling would keep many Poles from entering the labour market.

"Longer schooling periods and early retirements are likely to keep the supply of labour from growing faster than the Polish economy can absorb in the medium-term," said Witkowski, a leading Polish labour market economist.
Unemployment is unlikely to be a major issue in Poland's parliamentary elections later this year, some analysts said.

Economists said unemployment in the longer-term hinged largely on how well the 12-million-strong rural community adjusted to the inevitable switch from small, subsistence farms to ones producing EU quality produce.
They said about half of the two million farms were expected to fail as Poland restructured its agriculture for EU entry.
"Whether bankrupt farmers can find employment without leaving their rural areas is a key to keeping Polish unemployment levels from growing," Witkowski said.

Economists said agricultural areas, which had largely underdeveloped service and retail sectors under communism, had shown a remarkable ability to grow during the last few years despite low capital investment.

"Capital is not interested in rural areas, but such investment is the only way to create non-farming jobs and slowly enable the government to cut agriculture subsidies," said Adam Czyzewski, head of the independent NOBE think-tank.
Economists said investment in infrastructure, especially housing and transport sectors, would further cut unemployment levels as it would enable the workforce to become more mobile.

"Low labour costs -- presently one-tenth of those in Germany -- and EU entry will continue to bring large amounts of capital to Poland and keep demand for labour high, making the unemployment outlook positive," Witkowski predicted. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
